segments.text: Nahī̃ and maiṁ are already in your mouth. Today they arrive on the page.
First, say the last things you learned once more, out loud and from memory:

segments.instruction: tuhāḍā nāṁ kī hai?, khushī hoī

segments.text: ਨ.
nannā — na. A consonant, the dental n: the tongue touches the teeth, not the ridge behind them.
bihārī — -ī. A mātrā for the long ee of see. It stands to the right and hooks back over the head-line.
dulāvā̃ — -ai. A mātrā built from two strokes above the line — dulāvā̃ means “the double lāvā̃.”
Now put them where you have already heard them:
ਨ + ਹ + ੀ + ਂ becomes ਨਹੀਂ (nahī̃) ਮ + ੈ + ਂ becomes ਮੈਂ (maiṁ, “I”) ਨਹੀਂ — nahī̃ — no.
You are not being asked to write any of this. You are being asked to recognise it the next time it goes past.

lessons.title: ਕਿਵੇਂ (kivēṁ) — "how," another of the k- questions

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: You met ਕੀ (kī, "what") in Chapter 2. Here is its sibling — and, like all of Punjabi's question-words, it starts with k-.
ਕ (ka) + ਿ (the sihārī, i-sign, written before) becomes ਕਿ (ki); ਵ (va) + ੇ (e-sign) + ਂ (nasal) becomes ਵੇਂ (vēṁ). Read ਕਿ, ਵੇਂ becomes kivēṁ.

ਕਿਵੇਂ (kivēṁ, "how") is from the interrogative stem ka-, from PIE kʷo- — the same question-root behind English wh- and Latin qu-. Punjabi's questions nearly all begin with this k-: kī (what), kauṇ (who), kad (when), kithē (where), kivēṁ (how). Learn the k- and you can spot a question.

the k- question family — kī, kauṇ, kad, kithē, kivēṁ

lessons.title: ਤੁਸੀਂ ਕਿਵੇਂ ਹੋ? (tusī̃ kivēṁ ho?) — "how are you?"

segments.text: Three words you own, assembled into the first thing you ask after hello.

ਤੁਸੀਂ ਕਿਵੇਂ ਹੋ? (tusī̃ kivēṁ ho?) = ਤੁਸੀਂ (tusī̃, respectful "you") + ਕਿਵੇਂ (kivēṁ, "how") + ਹੋ (ho, "are") — literally "you how are?" Punjabi keeps the verb last, as in Chapter 2. The copula ho is the respectful "are" that goes with tusī̃ — its whole set is maiṁ hāṁ (I am), tū̃ haiṁ (you are, familiar), oh hai (he is), tusī̃ ho (you are, respectful).

segments.text: To an elder or stranger: tusī̃ kivēṁ ho? To a friend: tū̃ kivēṁ haiṁ? Respect takes the plural-shaped tusī̃ … ho.

lessons.title: ਮੈਂ (maiṁ) — "I," the m- of the first person

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: To answer "how are you?" you first need "I." In Chapter 2 you learned merā ("my"); here is its owner.
ਮ (ma) + ੈ (ai-sign) + ਂ (nasal bindi) becomes ਮੈਂ (maiṁ). One nasal syllable.

ਮੈਂ (maiṁ, "I") is on the first-person root ma- — the same root that gave you merā ("my"), and the same m- behind English me, my, mine and Latin mē. Punjabi's "I," its "my," and English's "me/my" all grow from one ancient first-person sound.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the copula pairs with it

segments.text: Maiṁ takes the copula ਹਾਂ (hāṁ, "am"): maiṁ … hāṁ. Watch out — this hāṁ ("am") is spelled the same as the hāṁ ("yes") from Chapter 1; context tells them apart. So the reply to "how are you?" will begin maiṁ …

segments.instruction: "maiṁ"
the m- family — maiṁ (I), merā (my), English me, my
"maiṁ … hāṁ" — I am …

segments.text: What root links maiṁ, merā, and English me, and what copula does maiṁ take? (The first-person ma-; hāṁ, "am.")

feedback.correct: Right: maiṁ means I, and its copula frame ends in hāṁ.
feedback.incorrect: Use maiṁ for I and finish the frame with hāṁ, am.

segments.text: English has no letter for any of these. The tongue curls back to the roof of the mouth for all three.
First, say the last things you learned once more, out loud and from memory:

segments.instruction: tusī̃ kivēṁ ho?, tusī̃ kivēṁ ho — k-, maiṁ

blocks.title: Script you'll notice: ਟ, ਠ, ਡ

segments.text: ਟ.
ṭaiṅkā — ṭa. A retroflex t, with no breath: the tongue curls back and taps the roof of the mouth.
ਠ.
ṭhaṭṭhā — ṭha. A retroflex t with a puff of breath: tongue curled back to the roof of the mouth.
ਡ.
ḍaḍḍā — ḍa. A retroflex d, the voiced partner of ṭaiṅkā.
Now put them where you have already heard them:
ਟ ਠ ਡ — one row, one tongue position, three degrees of breath and voice ਠ + ੀ + ਕ becomes ਠੀਕ (ṭhīk) ਠੀਕ — ṭhīk — fine, all right.
You are not being asked to write any of this. You are being asked to recognise it the next time it goes past.

lessons.title: ਠੀਕ (ṭhīk) — "fine," and how to answer
lessons.gloss: fine, well — and the reply maiṁ ṭhīk hāṁ

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: The word that answers "how are you?" — and does a dozen other jobs.
ਠ (ṭha, a retroflex th — tongue curled to the roof of the mouth) + ੀ (long ī) + ਕ (ka) becomes ਠੀਕ (ṭhīk). The retroflex ਟ-ਠ-ਡ series is a hallmark of Indian sound.

ਠੀਕ (ṭhīk) means "correct, right, fine, OK" — a native Indian word (shared with Hindi and Urdu), one of the most useful in the language: ṭhīk hai ("OK / agreed"), sab ṭhīk? ("all well?"). Not every word has a far-flung cognate, and that is worth seeing too: ṭhīk is Indian to the core.
Put it together: ਮੈਂ ਠੀਕ ਹਾਂ (maiṁ ṭhīk hāṁ) — "I am fine" (literally "I fine am," verb last). Add thanks: maiṁ ṭhīk hāṁ, dhannavād. The whole exchange:
— tusī̃ kivēṁ ho? ("How are you?") — maiṁ ṭhīk hāṁ, dhannavād. ("I'm fine, thank you.")

lessons.title: ਕੋਈ ਗੱਲ ਨਹੀਂ (koī gall nahīṁ) — "it's nothing"
lessons.gloss: it is nothing; no problem; you are welcome

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: When someone thanks you — or apologises — this is the easy, gracious reply, built on a word from Chapter 1.
ਕੋਈ (koī, "any") + ਗੱਲ (gall, "matter, talk" — note the addak, the doubling mark, on ੱਲ) + ਨਹੀਂ (nahīṁ, "not," from Chapter 1) becomes koī gall nahīṁ.

ਕੋਈ ਗੱਲ ਨਹੀਂ (koī gall nahīṁ) literally means "[there is] no matter" — koī ("any") + gall ("matter, thing, talk") + nahīṁ ("not"). It serves as "it's nothing / no worries / never mind / you're welcome." The word ਗੱਲ (gall, "talk, matter") is a warm, everyday native Punjabi word — gall karnā ("to have a chat"). And ਨਹੀਂ (nahīṁ) you already met in Chapter 1: the ancient negative na-, the same PIE ne behind English no, not, none.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — roots you now carry

segments.text: kivēṁ from the interrogative k- (PIE kʷo-), cousin of English how/what.
maiṁ from ma- (PIE me-), cousin of English me/my.
ṭhīk — native Indian "fine," no European cognate.
koī gall nahīṁ — "no matter"; nahīṁ from PIE ne, English no.
A stranger asks tusī̃ kivēṁ ho? — give a full, polite reply, and answer their thanks. (Maiṁ ṭhīk hāṁ, dhannavād — and to thanks, koī gall nahīṁ.)

Independent Gurmukhi reading and writing are not scored here. Chapter 3 still contains untaught forms; #13068 must build their visible-model, guided-copy, delayed-copy, and dictation runway before either skill can earn credit. A romanized answer never counts as Gurmukhi writing.
